4490: Discretion has two closely related meanings, and both revolve around one central idea: good judgment. One meaning is about how you behave (carefully and wisely), and the other is about the power you have (the freedom to make your own call).
Meaning 1: Careful, Tactful, and Private Behavior

This is the more common everyday meaning. When someone shows discretion, it means they are careful and wise about what they say, what they share, and how they act — especially in sensitive or delicate situations.

Think of it this way: some information is private, some situations are fragile, and some moments require you to stay quiet rather than speak up. A person who handles these moments with discretion knows exactly what to say, what not to say, and how to behave so that no harm, embarrassment, or damage is caused.

Key qualities that make up discretion in this sense:

  • Knowing when to keep quiet. If your friend tells you something personal and asks you not to share it, and you don't — that's discretion.
  • Not drawing unnecessary attention. If you notice your colleague made a mistake in a meeting, discretion means you bring it up privately later rather than calling them out in front of everyone.
  • Being trustworthy with sensitive information. A doctor knows private things about patients. A lawyer knows private things about clients. They are expected to handle that information with discretion — meaning they don't gossip, don't share carelessly, and treat it with respect.
  • Reading the room. Discretion also involves knowing when a topic is inappropriate, when a joke is out of place, or when silence is wiser than speech.

Examples:

  • "She showed great discretion by not mentioning the argument in front of the children."
  • "The journalist used discretion and chose not to publish certain details that could harm innocent people."
  • "He handled the scandal with discretion, avoiding unnecessary drama."
  • "We need someone who can be trusted to act with discretion in this role."

The opposite of this kind of discretion is being indiscreet — blurting things out, sharing secrets, saying the wrong thing at the wrong time, or handling sensitive matters carelessly.
Meaning 2: The Freedom or Power to Make Your Own Judgment

The second meaning shifts from behavior to authority and freedom. Here, discretion means the right or power to decide something yourself, based on your own judgment — without being forced to follow a strict rule.

When someone has discretion over something, it means the decision is theirs to make. There is no single fixed answer. They get to weigh the situation and choose what they think is best.

Examples:

  • "The judge has discretion when it comes to sentencing — she can give a lighter or heavier penalty based on the specific case."
  • "Employees are given discretion over how they organize their workday."
  • "The scholarship committee has full discretion in selecting the winner."
  • "Tips are left at the customer's discretion." (Meaning: it's entirely up to the customer to decide.)

This is where the very common phrase "at someone's discretion" comes from. It simply means: it's up to that person to decide.

  • "Dress code is at the manager's discretion." → The manager decides.
  • "Extra credit is awarded at the teacher's discretion." → The teacher decides, case by case.
  • "Entry is at the bouncer's discretion." → The bouncer makes the call.

Another common instruction you'll hear is "use your discretion" — which means: don't wait for someone to spell out every rule; use your own good judgment to figure out what's right in this situation.

At first glance, these two meanings might seem unrelated. But they share a deep common thread: judgment.

  • In Meaning 1, discretion means using good judgment about how to behave — what to say, what to keep quiet, how to handle sensitive things wisely.
  • In Meaning 2, discretion means having the authority to use your own judgment — the power to make a decision without being forced down a fixed path.

In both cases, the word is pointing toward a person who thinks carefully, reads situations well, and acts wisely rather than rashly.

"With discretion"
Means carefully, privately, and tactfully.
"Please handle this matter with discretion."

"At someone's discretion"
Means it is up to that person to decide.
"Refunds are issued at the manager's discretion."

"Use your discretion"
Means make your own wise judgment.
"The guidelines are flexible — just use your discretion."

"Discretion is advised"
A warning that the content ahead may be sensitive, and you should judge whether it's appropriate for you (or those around you).
"Viewer discretion is advised" — a phrase you often see before mature content on television.

"Discretion is the better part of valor"
A well-known proverb meaning that it is sometimes wiser and braver to be cautious and hold back than to act boldly. True courage includes knowing when not to act.

• Discreet (adjective): The describing word. A discreet person is one who has discretion — careful, tactful, and trustworthy. "She was very discreet about what she knew."
  • Indiscretion (noun): The opposite of discretion — a careless, thoughtless act or remark, especially one that reveals something private. "His indiscretion cost him his career."
  • Discretionary (adjective): Describes something that is left to someone's own judgment or choice. "Discretionary spending" means money you choose to spend (as opposed to money you must spend on necessities).
A Quick Way to Remember It

Think of discretion as having two faces, one soul:

Face 1 → "I know what NOT to say or do here." (careful, private behavior)

Face 2 → "It's MY call to make." (freedom of judgment)

Both faces show a person who is thoughtful, trusted, and wise. That's the soul of the word.
4491:
Something is discretionary when it is not fixed, not forced, and not automatic — it depends entirely on the judgment and choice of the person or authority who has the power to decide.

In other words: no rule, law, or obligation requires it to happen in a particular way. The decision is left open, and whoever holds the relevant authority gets to decide whether to act, how much to act, or when to act — based on their own assessment of the situation.

The clearest way to grasp "discretionary" is by placing it next to its opposite.

  • Mandatory (compulsory): Must happen. There is no choice. The outcome is pre-determined by a rule, law, or contract.
  • Discretionary: May or may not happen, or may happen to varying degrees. The outcome depends on someone's judgment.

If your employer is required by law to pay you a certain minimum wage, that payment is mandatory — not discretionary. But if your employer chooses to give you a year-end bonus based on how well the company performed and how they feel about your work, that bonus is discretionary — they decide its size, or even whether to give it at all.
What Makes Something "Discretionary"? Two Things Working Together

When we call something discretionary, two ideas are always present:

  1. Freedom: There is genuine latitude to choose. No external rule locks the outcome in advance.
  2. Judgment: That freedom isn't random or arbitrary. The person exercising it is expected to think carefully and decide wisely. Discretionary power comes with an implied responsibility to use good judgment.

This is an important nuance. Discretionary does not mean "whatever you feel like." It means: you have the freedom to decide, and you're expected to decide thoughtfully.
Where You'll See This Word Used

1. Money and Finance

This is one of the most common areas.

  • Discretionary income / discretionary spending: The money left over after you've paid for all your necessities — rent, food, utilities, loan repayments. Because you are not obligated to spend this money on any particular thing, it is "discretionary." You can save it, travel with it, spend it on entertainment, or do anything you judge best. No bill is waiting for it.
  • Discretionary budget: A portion of a company's or government's budget that is not pre-committed to fixed expenses. It can be allocated at the decision-maker's judgment — to new projects, emergencies, or opportunities that arise.
  • Discretionary bonus: A bonus that an employer is not contractually required to pay. Whether they give it, and how much, is entirely up to their decision. Because it's not guaranteed, you can't count on it the way you count on your fixed salary.
  • Discretionary fund: A reserve of money that a person or organization can use at their own discretion, without needing prior approval or being bound to spend it on specific things.

2. Authority and Power (Law, Government, Management)

  • Discretionary powers / discretionary authority: When a judge, police officer, government official, or manager is given "discretionary powers," it means they are authorized to make decisions on a case-by-case basis using their own judgment. The rules don't dictate a single mandatory outcome; they give the authority figure room to weigh the circumstances and decide.
    For example: A judge may have discretionary authority in sentencing. Two people may commit the same crime, but the judge can look at each person's circumstances — history, intent, remorse — and choose a sentence they find appropriate, within legal limits. The sentence is not mechanically pre-determined.
  • Discretionary decision: Any decision that is made based on the decision-maker's own judgment rather than by following a fixed rule.

3. Everyday and General Use

  • "Attendance at the optional seminar is discretionary." (You decide whether to go — no one is forcing you.)
  • "The doctor may, at her discretionary judgment, prescribe a lower dose." (She has the freedom and responsibility to decide what's right for the patient.)
  • "Tipping at restaurants is generally discretionary." (No law requires it; you decide whether to tip and how much, based on your judgment of the service.)

This matters because learners sometimes misread it:

  • It does not mean "unimportant." Discretionary decisions can be very significant. A judge's discretionary sentencing decision can affect someone's entire life.
  • It does not mean "random" or "arbitrary." A discretionary choice is made by a thinking person using judgment. It's the opposite of random — it's considered.
  • It does not mean "definitely won't happen." It means it might or might not happen, or the amount isn't fixed. The person with the authority decides.
  • It does not mean "optional in a lazy sense." It means the obligation is open-ended and judgment-dependent, not that the matter is trivial.

One useful thing to notice is that discretionary power can be wide or narrow.

  • Wide discretionary power: "The committee may allocate these funds however it sees fit." → Almost unlimited judgment.
  • Narrow discretionary power: "The officer may issue a warning instead of a fine, but only for first-time offenders." → Judgment allowed, but within tight conditions.

In both cases, the word "discretionary" still applies — but the scope of freedom differs. Context usually tells you how wide or narrow that freedom is.

Discretionary = left to someone's own judgment and choice, rather than being fixed, automatic, or mandatory.

When something is discretionary, no pre-set rule determines the outcome. A person or authority with the relevant power gets to look at the situation, weigh it, and decide — whether to act, how much, or in what way. That freedom always comes paired with an expectation of good judgment.
4492:
The adjective discriminate means: carefully selective; making thoughtful distinctions. It describes something (or someone) that is not random, not careless, but precise — showing the ability to tell things apart and choose wisely among them.

Think of it this way: to discriminate between things means to recognize real differences between them. So when you describe something as discriminate, you're saying it reflects that careful, deliberate recognition of differences.
What It Really Means — Going Deeper

The adjective carries two closely related ideas bundled together:

1. Selectivity — not grabbing everything indiscriminately, but choosing with purpose.
2. Discernment — the ability to notice fine distinctions that others might miss.

When a person or action is called discriminate, it signals a kind of intellectual precision — the quality of being able to separate the good from the bad, the relevant from the irrelevant, the worthy from the unworthy.

A discriminate reader doesn't read every book thrown at them — they read thoughtfully, selecting books that deserve their attention.

A discriminate use of language means choosing words carefully, with awareness of their exact meaning — not using them loosely or carelessly.

• "She was a discriminate collector of antiques, buying only pieces with genuine historical value."
    (She didn't buy randomly; she had the judgment to distinguish truly valuable items from imposters.)
  • "The general issued discriminate orders — only specific targets were to be engaged, nothing indiscriminate."
    (The orders were precise and selective, not broad and sweeping.)
  • "His discriminate praise made it all the more meaningful — he didn't compliment everyone."
    (He praised only what truly deserved praise, so when he said something was good, you knew he meant it.)
  • "A discriminate mind approaches problems methodically, separating facts from assumptions."
    (A careful, precise mind — one that draws sharp distinctions.)

This is important to understand. In everyday speech, the verb "to discriminate" often carries a negative meaning — treating someone unfairly because of their race, gender, religion, etc. But the adjective form is positive (or at worst neutral).

Calling someone discriminate is a compliment. It means they have good judgment. They are not easily fooled. They can tell quality from mediocrity, truth from falsehood, the essential from the trivial.

The cleanest way to understand any word is through its opposite, and here the contrast is very sharp.

Indiscriminate = random, without distinction, careless, making no effort to separate one thing from another.
Discriminate = the exact opposite — deliberate, precise, making careful distinctions.

An indiscriminate bombing attacks everything — civilians, military targets, fields, hospitals — without distinction. A discriminate bombing (in theory) targets only specific military objectives, avoiding everything else.

An indiscriminate eater will eat anything put in front of them. A discriminate eater notices flavor, texture, quality — and chooses accordingly.

You will often encounter the closely related adjective discriminating, which carries almost the same meaning and is arguably more commonly used in modern English.

  • A discriminating reader = a discriminate reader
  • A discriminating palate = an ability to detect fine differences in taste

Both words point to the same quality. "Discriminating" emphasizes the active exercise of that judgment; "discriminate" emphasizes that the choice or action itself reflects such judgment. In practice, the two are nearly interchangeable in most contexts.

What it meansCareful, thoughtful, selective; showing the ability to tell things apart and make precise distinctions
TonePositive — a mark of intelligence, taste, and good judgment
Who or what can be "discriminate"?A person's taste, judgment, choices, praise, reading habits, use of language, actions, etc.
Key quality it signalsPrecision over randomness; thought over carelessness

The adjective discriminate essentially honors the human capacity to see clearly — to not lump everything together, to resist the lazy impulse to treat all things as equal, and instead to recognize real differences with care and intelligence.
4493:
Discriminate means to notice a difference and act on it — either by telling things apart, or by treating people differently based on some characteristic.

That one core idea — noticing a difference and acting on it — splits into two very distinct uses, and it's crucial to understand both.

In this sense, discriminate simply means to recognize or identify the difference between two or more things. There is nothing negative about it here.

Pattern: discriminate between things

Examples:

  • A professional wine taster can discriminate between a cheap wine and an expensive one just by smell.
  • A good doctor can discriminate between a viral infection and a bacterial one.
  • Young children often cannot discriminate between fantasy and reality.

Here, discriminating is actually a skill. It means you are sharp enough to notice differences that others might miss. Think of it as the mental act of sorting — your brain is carefully separating one thing from another based on real, observable differences.

This is the more commonly heard use today, and it carries a strongly negative meaning. Here, discriminate means to treat a person or group of people unfairly or unequally based on a characteristic they belong to — such as their race, gender, religion, age, disability, nationality, or sexual orientation.

Pattern: discriminate against someone

Examples:

  • The company was sued for discriminating against women during the hiring process.
  • It is illegal in many countries to discriminate against people because of their religion.
  • He felt he was being discriminated against at work because of his age.

Notice the key phrase: "discriminate against." This tells you straight away that you are in the negative sense of the word. Someone is being treated worse — denied a job, excluded from a place, denied rights, or treated with hostility — not because of anything they did, but simply because of who they are or what group they belong to.

The critical thing here is that the difference being acted upon is unjust and irrelevant. A company might say "we don't hire people over 50" — the person's age has nothing fair to do with their ability to do the job. That is discrimination.
The Key Difference Between the Two Senses

Both senses involve noticing a difference and acting on it, but here is what separates them:

Sense 1 (neutral): The differences you notice are real and relevant, and you are simply exercising judgment or perception. A chef discriminates between fresh and stale ingredients — the difference genuinely matters.

Sense 2 (negative): The characteristic you act on is irrelevant to the situation, and someone is treated worse because of it. An employer discriminating against a candidate because of their skin color — the skin color has nothing to do with the job.

In short: one is a skill, the other is an injustice.

When the word is used as an adjective — a discriminating person — it almost always means someone who has refined taste and sharp judgment. It comes from Sense 1.

  • She is a discriminating reader — she knows good writing from bad.
  • He has a discriminating eye for art — he can spot quality and flaw alike.

This is a compliment. A discriminating person is someone who doesn't accept everything at face value; they can tell the excellent from the mediocre.

Since you'll encounter this closely, it's worth noting: the noun form is discrimination, and it follows the same two senses.

  • "Color discrimination" — the ability of the eye to tell colors apart (Sense 1, neutral).
  • "Racial discrimination" — treating people unequally based on race (Sense 2, negative).

In everyday conversation, when people say "discrimination" without any qualifier, they almost always mean the negative sense — unfair treatment of people.
Common Collocations (Words That Go With It)

These are the most natural word pairings you'll see:

  • discriminate between → used in the neutral sense (discriminate between right and wrong)
  • discriminate against → used in the negative sense (discriminate against minorities)
  • racial / gender / age / religious discrimination → specifies what the unfair treatment is based on
  • a discriminating taste / eye / palate → high standards and sharp judgment (always positive)

Discriminate between thingsNeutral — to notice and tell apart real differences. A skill.
Discriminate against peopleNegative — to treat unfairly based on irrelevant characteristics. An injustice.
Discriminating (adjective)Positive — having sharp judgment and refined taste.
One Sentence to Remember It All
Discriminate means to act on a noticed difference — wisely, when you use it to tell things apart; unjustly, when you use it to treat a person worse because of who they are.
4494:
When we call someone discriminating, we mean they have the sharp ability to notice fine differences between things — and because of that, they have excellent, refined taste and judgment. They don't just accept anything that comes their way. They carefully evaluate, compare, and choose only what is truly good or of high quality.

Think of it this way: imagine two people walking into an art gallery.

  • Person A glances around and says, "Yeah, these all look like nice paintings to me."
  • Person B studies each painting and says, "This one has exceptional brushwork, this one has a poorly balanced composition, and this one — this one is a masterpiece."

Person B is the discriminating one. They can see differences that others miss, and their judgment is sharper for it.

The word rests on two ideas working together:

1. The ability to tell things apart
A discriminating person can detect subtle differences — in quality, style, value, flavor, craftsmanship — that an ordinary or careless observer would completely overlook.

2. Refined selectivity as a result
Because they can tell things apart so well, they are very selective. They have high standards. They won't settle for something mediocre when they know what excellent looks like.

Together, these make "discriminating" a word that describes someone with a sophisticated, well-trained sense of quality and judgment.

"Discriminating" almost always appears before a noun, describing a person's faculty of judgment in a particular area. The most common combinations you'll encounter are:

  • A discriminating taste — someone who can tell the difference between good food, wine, music, or art and something merely average.
  • A discriminating eye — someone who can visually spot quality, flaws, or excellence with precision.
  • A discriminating palate — specifically used for food and drink; someone who can detect subtle flavors others can't.
  • A discriminating reader — someone who critically evaluates what they read rather than accepting everything at face value.
  • A discriminating buyer/collector — someone who carefully selects only the finest items and won't be fooled by inferior goods.

• "The restaurant was designed to please even the most discriminating food lovers."

(It was so good, it could satisfy even people with very high, refined standards.)

  • "She was a discriminating collector who only purchased paintings she considered true masterpieces."

(She was so skilled at judging quality that she was very selective in what she bought.)

  • "The editor had a discriminating eye — he could spot a weak paragraph instantly, no matter how polished it appeared."

(His judgment was sharp enough to catch flaws others would miss.)

  • "Wine critics must have a discriminating palate to do their job well."

(They need the refined ability to detect subtle differences in flavor.)

This is important — "discriminating" in its adjective form is a positive, respectful word. Calling someone discriminating is a compliment. You are saying they have developed, refined judgment. You are saying they are not fooled easily. You are saying they know quality when they see it.

If someone says you have a "discriminating taste," they are praising you — suggesting that your sense of quality is so well-developed that you can spot what's genuinely good and reject what isn't.
What It Does NOT Mean (A Critical Distinction)

Here is where many learners get confused. You may know that "discrimination" can be a very negative word — as in treating people unfairly because of their race, gender, religion, etc. That is a completely different sense of the word.

When "discriminating" is used as an adjective to describe a person's taste, eye, palate, or judgment, it carries no negative meaning at all. It simply means having the refined ability to tell apart quality from mediocrity.

The negative social meaning belongs to the word "discriminatory" (e.g., "discriminatory policies"), not to "discriminating" in this adjective form.

Knowing these will help you see the word from different angles:

  • Discerning — the closest synonym; almost interchangeable
  • Selective — emphasizes being choosy and not accepting just anything
  • Perceptive — able to notice things others miss
  • Refined — having cultured, polished taste
  • Particular — very careful and exact about choices
  • Fastidious — extremely attentive to quality and detail (slightly stronger)
  • Judicious — showing sound judgment

• Undiscriminating — accepting anything without careful judgment
  • Indiscriminate — making choices randomly or carelessly, without considering quality or distinctions
  • Unselective — not choosy; accepting whatever comes
A Simple Mental Image to Lock It In

Picture a jeweler examining diamonds. While most people just see a shiny stone, the jeweler holds it under a loupe and can immediately spot the cut quality, the clarity, the tiny flaws, and the brilliance that separates a gem worth $500 from one worth $50,000.

That jeweler is discriminating. Their trained perception allows them to see what others cannot — and that refined judgment makes them highly selective in what they approve of.

Whenever you see the word "discriminating" used as an adjective, picture that jeweler: someone whose judgment is sharp enough to see what others miss, and selective enough to choose only the finest.
4495: "Discrimination" has two distinct meanings that are both in active use today. Understanding both is essential, because using or hearing the word without knowing which meaning is intended can lead to real confusion.
Meaning 1 — The Neutral Sense: Noticing Differences

"Discrimination" simply means the ability to recognize and tell apart differences between things. This is the older, more neutral sense of the word, and it carries no judgment — it is actually a sign of intelligence and sharpness.

When used this way, it means a kind of careful, precise perception — the skill of noticing subtle distinctions that others might miss.

Examples:

  • A professional wine taster has a discrimination of flavors that most people lack. (She can tell a wine from France apart from one from Italy just by taste.)
  • A skilled editor has a discrimination for language — she can spot awkward phrasing that looks perfectly fine to others.
  • "His discrimination in choosing art for the gallery is remarkable." (He picks pieces with a trained, careful eye.)

When someone is called "a discriminating person" in this sense, it is a compliment. It means they have refined, exacting taste and judgment — they don't accept just anything.
Meaning 2 — The Social Sense: Unfair Treatment of People

This is the meaning most people think of today, and it is the far more common one in everyday conversation. Here, "discrimination" means treating a person or group of people unfairly or unequally because of who they are, not because of anything they have actually done or earned.

The key idea: a person is judged not on their own merits, actions, or abilities, but on a characteristic they belong to — such as their race, gender, religion, age, disability, nationality, sexual orientation, or social class.

Examples:

  • A company refuses to hire a qualified woman simply because she is a woman. That is gender discrimination.
  • A landlord refuses to rent to a family because of their religion. That is religious discrimination.
  • A person is paid less than a colleague doing the same job, purely because of their skin color. That is racial discrimination.
  • An older employee is passed over for promotion only because of their age. That is age discrimination.

In all of these cases, the characteristic being used (gender, religion, race, age) has nothing to do with the person's ability to do the job or meet the requirement. That is what makes it discrimination — the judgment is irrelevant and unfair.
The Different Forms Discrimination Can Take

Discrimination in this social sense doesn't always show up in an obvious, direct way. It can be subtle or even unintentional:

Direct discrimination is the most straightforward kind. Someone is treated worse than others explicitly because of a characteristic. "We don't hire people from that community" is direct discrimination stated openly.

Indirect discrimination is trickier. A rule or policy applies equally to everyone on the surface, but in practice it puts a particular group at a significant disadvantage — and there is no good reason for it. For example: a company requires all employees to work on Sundays with no exceptions. This seems neutral, but it puts Christians (for whom Sunday is a day of worship) at a disadvantage that doesn't apply to others.

Systemic or institutional discrimination is when discrimination is baked into the way an entire system, organization, or society operates — not just one person's attitude. It means the structures and rules themselves produce unequal outcomes for certain groups, even when no single person may be acting with conscious prejudice.

You may sometimes hear the phrase positive discrimination (in British English) or affirmative action (in American English). This refers to deliberately favoring a group that has historically been disadvantaged or underrepresented — for example, giving preference in hiring or university admissions to people from marginalized backgrounds. The intention is to correct existing inequality.

This is controversial: supporters argue it is a necessary tool to level an uneven playing field; critics argue that favoring one group over another, even with good intentions, is itself a form of unfairness. The word "positive" here is used to signal the intent is corrective rather than harmful — though whether it is actually "positive" is a matter of genuine debate.
The Critical Distinction Between the Two Meanings

Here is the clearest way to hold both meanings in your mind at once:

  • In Meaning 1, you are discriminating between things — wine, art, arguments, quality. You are using your judgment to tell apart what is good from what is poor, based on relevant qualities. This is a skill, and it is good.
  • In Meaning 2, you are discriminating against people — treating them worse based on characteristics like race or gender that are irrelevant to the situation at hand. This is a harm, and it is unjust.

The shared thread is the idea of drawing a distinction. But in Meaning 1, the distinction is made carefully and fairly, based on what actually matters. In Meaning 2, the distinction is made unjustly, based on what doesn't matter.
A Final Note on Degree and Context

Discrimination in the social sense exists on a spectrum. It can be:

  • Overt — openly stated, aggressive, and intentional
  • Subtle — hidden in microaggressions, assumptions, or tone
  • Unconscious (implicit bias) — when a person discriminates without being fully aware that they are doing so; their deep-seated assumptions shape their behavior without their conscious knowledge

Discrimination also matters legally. In most democratic countries, discrimination on the basis of race, gender, religion, disability, and several other characteristics is illegal in employment, housing, and public services. This is why the word appears so often in law, journalism, and public policy discussions.

In short: discrimination either means the sharp ability to tell things apart (a positive quality of mind) or the unfair treatment of people based on irrelevant characteristics (a social wrong). Context — especially whether the subject is a person being treated a certain way or a quality someone possesses — almost always makes clear which meaning is intended.
4496: Discursive is an adjective with two distinct meanings. They feel different on the surface, but share a common soul — the idea of a mind that is moving through something rather than staying in one place.
Meaning 1 — Wandering from topic to topic (everyday usage)

This is the meaning you'll encounter most often.

When writing, speech, or thought is described as discursive, it means it wanders. It drifts from one subject to another without following a tight, focused, straight-line path. A discursive essay might begin with a reflection on loneliness, drift into the history of letter-writing, take a detour through Victorian social customs, and finally circle back to something loosely resembling its starting point. It covers a lot of ground — but not in a disciplined, direct way.

Think of the opposite: a focused, well-structured piece of writing that picks one clear point and drives straight toward it. Discursive writing is the opposite of that. It meanders the way a river does — it eventually gets somewhere, but it takes the scenic route, full of bends and side-channels.

A simple example:
Imagine a professor who starts a lecture on the French Revolution, then spends twenty minutes on the philosophy of Rousseau, then veers into a story about his grandmother's kitchen in Lyon, and eventually returns to Napoleon — but only in the last five minutes. His lecture is discursive. It was intellectually rich, perhaps, but it wandered.

Does discursive always mean bad?

Not at all. The word can carry a mildly critical tone when someone is calling out unfocused thinking. But it can also be completely neutral, or even a compliment. Many beloved writers — essayists especially — are deliberately discursive. Their work wanders on purpose, exploring ideas with curiosity and pleasure rather than rushing toward a conclusion. A discursive conversation between two thoughtful friends, jumping freely from memory to philosophy to food, can be one of the most enjoyable things in life. The word simply names the wandering quality. Whether that's a flaw or a charm depends entirely on context.
Meaning 2 — Proceeding step by step through reasoning (philosophical usage)

In philosophy, logic, and academic writing, discursive takes on a more specific and surprisingly different meaning.

Here, it describes thinking or knowledge that works through a chain of logical steps — moving from one point to the next, building an argument the way you climb a staircase: one step at a time, in sequence.

This meaning is always understood in contrast with intuitive knowledge. Intuitive knowledge arrives all at once — like a sudden flash of insight, a gut feeling that something is true without needing to be argued. Discursive knowledge is the opposite: it is deliberate, sequential, reasoned. You start with something you know, apply logic, derive a new conclusion, apply more logic, and keep going until you arrive at your answer by working through the argument methodically.

Solving a mathematical proof is a classic example of discursive thinking. You don't simply see the answer. You reason your way to it, step by step, each step justified by the one before it.

A simple example:
A mystic might claim to know God through a single overwhelming moment of inner experience — that is intuitive. A philosopher who tries to prove God's existence through a sequence of logical premises and deductions is being discursive. One arrives at knowledge in a flash; the other builds it like a careful argument.

At first glance, these two meanings look like they belong to completely different words. But look closer, and you'll find the same soul in both.

In the everyday sense, discursive thought moves sideways — from topic to topic, topic to topic, never settling.

In the philosophical sense, discursive thought moves forward — from premise to conclusion, step to step, through a chain of reasoning.

In both cases, the defining feature is that the mind is traveling through something. It is not resting on a single point. It is moving, covering territory, making a journey. That journey — whether it's a logical chain of reasoning or a wandering tour through loosely related ideas — is what makes something discursive.

Think of the word discourse — an extended piece of speaking or writing, a long treatment of a subject. Discursive is the adjective that captures the energy of discourse: it is the quality of something that extends, moves, travels through ideas or arguments, covers ground. If something is discursive, it is doing what a long, roaming discourse does — going places, not staying put.

In everyday use: wandering, loosely structured, moving from topic to topic without tight focus — used to describe writing, speech, or thinking that covers a lot of ground without driving in a straight line. Can be neutral or mildly critical depending on context.

In philosophy and academia: proceeding through logical steps and reasoning rather than arriving at knowledge by sudden intuition — describes careful, sequential, argument-based thought.

The thread connecting both: a mind in motion, traveling through.
4497:
A discussion is a focused, back-and-forth exchange of thoughts between two or more people on a specific topic. The people involved speak, listen, and respond to each other — sharing ideas, asking questions, raising points, or exploring different angles of a subject.

The key idea is exchange. A discussion is not one person talking while others just listen. Everyone involved contributes something, and what one person says influences what the next person says. It is interactive by nature.

For something to count as a discussion, it generally has these qualities:

It has a topic. A discussion is always about something — a problem, a plan, an event, a question, an idea. It is not random, aimless chatter.

It is two-way (or more). You cannot have a discussion by yourself. It requires at least two participants who are actively exchanging thoughts, not just taking turns speaking into the air.

It is relatively open. A discussion usually allows different perspectives to be heard. No one has declared a winner before it starts. The purpose is often to understand, explore, or examine — not necessarily to "beat" the other side.

It can be short or long, formal or informal. A five-minute chat with a friend about which movie to watch is a discussion. A three-hour boardroom meeting on company strategy is also a discussion. The word covers a wide range.

This is where many learners get confused, so let's be precise:

Discussion vs. Conversation
A conversation is a broad, general word for any talk between people — it can be about anything, with no particular goal, like chatting about the weather. A discussion is more focused. It has a specific subject and usually a purpose (to understand, decide, solve, or explore something). All discussions are conversations, but not all conversations are discussions.

Discussion vs. Debate
A debate is a structured contest of opposing views. The goal of a debate is to argue your side persuasively and, ideally, "win." There are clear opposing positions. A discussion is more collaborative — people are collectively examining a topic, not necessarily fighting for opposing teams. A discussion can have disagreement, but it is not built around opposition the way a debate is.

Discussion vs. Argument
An argument (in everyday use) often carries the sense of conflict — raised voices, frustration, people trying to overpower each other's views. A discussion is calmer, more reasoned, and more respectful, even when people disagree. You can disagree strongly in a discussion without it becoming an argument.

Discussion vs. Lecture / Presentation
A lecture or presentation is one-directional — one person speaks and the rest listen. A discussion is multi-directional. If a teacher stands and explains a topic to silent students, that is a lecture. If the teacher asks the class questions and students respond and build on each other's ideas, that is a discussion.

Discussion vs. Negotiation
A negotiation is a very specific kind of exchange aimed at reaching a practical agreement (like settling a price or resolving a conflict). A discussion is broader and may not lead to any concrete agreement — it may simply be an exploration of ideas.
How the word is used in academic and professional writing

In research papers, textbooks, and reports, Discussion often appears as a section heading. Here, it refers to the part of the writing where the author interprets findings or ideas — explaining what the results mean, what their implications are, how they connect to broader knowledge, and what limitations exist.

For example, a scientist might write: "This will be explored further in the Discussion section." This usage is more analytical and written, but the same underlying idea applies: a discussion is where things are examined and reflected upon, not just stated.

The word discussion can be used in both formal and informal settings without sounding out of place. However, it leans slightly formal compared to words like chat or talk.

  • Informal: "We had a quick discussion about the weekend plans."
  • Formal: "The committee held a lengthy discussion on the proposed budget."

Both are correct. The word fits comfortably in everyday speech, professional settings, academic writing, and journalism.

Here are the natural ways the word is used:

  • Have a discussion — the most common and natural phrase: "We need to have a discussion about this."
  • Hold a discussion — slightly more formal: "The school held a discussion on mental health."
  • Open / start / begin a discussion — to initiate one: "Her question opened a wider discussion about fairness."
  • Join a discussion — to become part of one already happening.
  • Under discussion — currently being talked about: "The proposal is still under discussion."
  • A lively / heated / brief / in-depth / open discussion — these adjectives show the character or depth of the discussion.
  • Discussion about / on / of something — all three prepositions are used: a discussion about climate change / on education policy / of the new rules.

• It is not a monologue (one person speaking without anyone responding).
  • It is not idle small talk with no focus or subject (that is called small talk or chatter).
  • It is not necessarily a conflict or fight, though it can include disagreement.
  • It does not always end with a resolution or decision — sometimes a discussion simply ends when the topic has been explored sufficiently.

1. "After a long discussion, the team decided to postpone the launch." — a focused exchange that led to a decision.
  2. "The documentary sparked a national discussion about inequality." — here, "discussion" refers to a large, widespread public conversation on a subject.
  3. "Can we schedule a discussion about your progress this week?" — a planned, purposeful exchange between two people.
  4. "The students had a rich discussion about the novel's ending." — a classroom exchange where multiple viewpoints were shared.
  5. "That topic is not up for discussion." — meaning it will not be talked about or reconsidered; it is closed.

Discussion captures the idea of minds meeting around a topic. It is purposeful, interactive, and open — a space where thoughts are exchanged rather than simply broadcast. Whether it happens between two friends, a classroom full of students, a panel of experts, or an author and their reader in a text, a discussion is always about the active, back-and-forth engagement with ideas.
4498:
Disdain is the feeling that someone or something is so inferior, unworthy, or beneath your standards that they don't deserve your respect, attention, or serious consideration.

It's not just disliking something. It's looking down on it — from a place of feeling superior.

Think of it like this: when you feel disdain, you're not just saying "I don't like this." You're saying, "This is too low, too cheap, too foolish, or too unworthy for someone like me to even bother with."

Disdain is always made of two things mixed together:

1. A sense of superiority — You see yourself (or your standards) as being on a higher level than the person or thing you're looking down on.

2. A dismissive attitude — Because you see them as inferior, you don't think they deserve your engagement, your energy, or your respect.

Remove either ingredient, and it stops being disdain. If you feel superior but still respect the other person, that's not disdain. If you dislike something but don't feel above it, that's not disdain either.
What Makes Disdain Unique (Its Emotional Texture)

One of the most important things to understand about disdain is that it is cold, not hot.

Anger is hot. Rage is hot. But disdain is cool and detached. A person feeling disdain doesn't usually shout or get emotional. Instead, they might:

  • Give a slow, withering look
  • Offer a slight, dismissive smile
  • Barely acknowledge the other person's existence
  • Respond in a clipped, uninterested way
  • Simply turn away, as if the person or thing isn't worth a full response

This coldness is what makes disdain feel so cutting. Being screamed at by someone feels bad, but being looked at with disdain feels worse in a different way — because it signals that you're not even worth the effort of strong emotion.
What Can You Feel Disdain For?

Disdain can be directed at many things:

  • A person — A wealthy aristocrat might treat a poor servant with disdain, barely acknowledging them as an equal.
  • A group of people — Someone might feel disdain for people they consider uneducated or unsophisticated.
  • Behavior or actions — A person of integrity might have disdain for lying and manipulation.
  • Objects or things — A fine chef might look at fast food with disdain.
  • Ideas — A serious scientist might feel disdain for conspiracy theories.
How Disdain Differs From Similar Words

These words are neighbors of disdain, but they're not the same:

Contempt is disdain's closest relative — they're almost identical. But contempt is usually stronger and more openly hostile. Disdain tends to be more quiet and detached. You might say contempt is disdain with more heat in it.

Scorn is disdain expressed out loud, often with mockery. Scorn is disdain that has decided to speak up and make the other person feel small. Disdain can stay silent; scorn rarely does.

Disgust is a gut-level, almost physical reaction — you feel it when something seems repulsive or revolting. Disdain is more of a social and intellectual feeling — about worth and status, not about being grossed out.

Disapproval is much milder. You can disapprove of a friend's decision while still fully respecting them. Disdain, on the other hand, always involves that sense of being above the person or thing.

These examples will show you how the word behaves naturally:

  • She looked at his handmade gift with barely concealed disdain, as if it were an embarrassment.
  • He had always felt disdain for people who cheated their way to the top.
  • The celebrity regarded the journalist's question with disdain — a brief glance, then silence.
  • There was open disdain in her voice when she spoke about those who broke promises.
  • He showed nothing but disdain for shortcuts — he believed in doing things properly, always.

• "With disdain" — She turned away with disdain. (Describes how an action is done.)
  • "Hold someone/something in disdain" — He held dishonesty in disdain. (To maintain a low opinion of something over time.)
  • "Treat with disdain" — She was treated with disdain by her so-called superiors.
  • "Look at with disdain" — He looked at the poor workmanship with disdain.
Is Disdain Always a Negative Thing?

Mostly, yes — disdain implies arrogance, and it's usually considered an uncharitable or snobbish attitude, especially when directed at people based on class, wealth, or social status.

However, disdain isn't always morally wrong. It can sometimes be a reasonable, even righteous response. A kind, honest person might feel disdain for cruelty, cowardice, or deliberate deception — and that kind of disdain reflects a principled refusal to respect behavior that genuinely doesn't deserve respect.

So context matters. Who is feeling disdain, toward what, and why — those answers determine whether the disdain is snobbery or integrity.
Disdain is the cold, quiet feeling that someone or something is inferior and unworthy of your respect — and the dismissive attitude that comes along with that feeling.
4499:
To disdain something means to look down on it as unworthy of your attention, respect, or effort — because you believe it is beneath you. It is a feeling of cold, superior contempt.

Notice two things packed into that meaning: you feel above something, and you treat it as not worth your time. Both parts matter. Disdain is not just dislike. It is dislike mixed with a sense of superiority.

Think of a very proud, dignified person. When they encounter something they consider low, cheap, or beneath their standards — they do not get angry or upset. They simply dismiss it with a cool, composed attitude, the way you might brush dust off your sleeve. They don't even think it deserves a strong reaction. That quiet, superior dismissal is exactly what disdain feels like.

This is important: disdain is not hot or explosive. It is cool and distant. A person full of rage hates something. A person full of disdain thinks something is simply too small, too common, or too weak to be taken seriously.

1. To disdain something or someone

Here, you use disdain to describe the attitude of looking down on a person, a thing, an idea, or a behavior.

  • She disdained gossip — she considered it beneath her to engage in petty talk.
  • The general disdained the enemy's threats — he saw them as weak and not worth worrying about.
  • He disdained people who cheated to win — he viewed them with contempt, as people of low character.

2. To disdain to do something

Here, disdain means to refuse to do something, because you feel it is beneath your dignity. This is a proud, deliberate refusal — not because you can't do it, but because you feel it is below you.

  • She disdained to reply to such a foolish question — she felt the question was so beneath her that answering it would almost be an insult to herself.
  • He disdained to beg for forgiveness — he was too proud to lower himself to begging.
  • The queen disdained to acknowledge the insult — she felt that reacting would give the insult more importance than it deserved.
How Disdain Differs from Similar Words

These words are close neighbors, but they are not identical.

Despise means to feel strong contempt or hatred for something. It is more emotionally intense and personal than disdain. You despise something deeply; you disdain something from a distance, as if it's not even worth your full emotional energy. Disdain is colder and more detached.

Scorn is the closest word to disdain and is often used interchangeably. However, scorn tends to be more openly expressed — it can be shown in a mocking laugh, a sneer, or a sharp remark. Disdain can be entirely silent and internal, communicated through indifference rather than mockery.

Contempt is the feeling of believing something or someone is worthless and deserving of no respect. Think of contempt as the emotion, and disdain as both the emotion and the behavior that comes from it. When you disdain something, contempt is usually the feeling fueling it.

Look down on is the casual, everyday phrase that means roughly the same thing as disdain, but disdain is more formal and carries a stronger literary and emotional weight.
The Character of Someone Who Disdains

A person who disdains things often carries a strong sense of their own worth or superiority — whether that is earned (a seasoned professional who disdains sloppy work) or arrogant and unfair (a wealthy person who disdains the poor). Disdain can belong to admirable people with high standards, or to deeply flawed people with an unjustified sense of superiority. The word itself does not judge — it simply describes the attitude.
The Tone and Register of This Word

Disdain is a formal, literary word. You will rarely hear it in casual conversation — people in everyday life would say "look down on," "can't stand," or "think they're too good for." You will encounter disdain most often in novels, essays, formal writing, or reporting where the writer wants to convey that particular flavor of cool, superior contempt with precision.

Because of its formal tone, using the word disdain in your own writing gives your language a sense of sophistication and sharpness.

If you want one mental image to anchor this word forever: picture a queen slowly turning her face away from something she finds beneath her — not in anger, not in fear, but with a calm, composed expression that says "this is not worthy of me." That silent, proud turning away is disdain in its purest form.
